{{short description|Infinite Cardinal number}}
In [[mathematics]], particularly in [[set theory]], the '''beth numbers''' form a certain (unset) sequence of [[infinite set|infinite]] [[cardinal number]]s (also known as [[transfinite number]]s), conventionally written <math>\beth_0, \beth_1, \beth_2, \beth_3, \dots</math>, where <math>\beth</math> is the [[Hebrew alphabet|Hebrew letter]] [[bet (letter)|beth]]. The beth numbers are related to the [[aleph number]]s (<math>\aleph_0, \aleph_1, \dots</math>), but unless the [[generalized continuum hypothesis]] is true, there are numbers indexed by <math>\aleph</math> that are not indexed by <math>\beth</math>. On the other hand, beth numbers are cofinal (every cardinal number is less than a beth number) in plain Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory.

== Definition ==
Beth numbers are indexed by [[ordinal number]]s and defined in terms of [[Von Neumann universe|the cumulative hierarchy]] by <math>\beth_\alpha = |V_{\omega+\alpha}|</math>, where <math>|A|</math> is the cardinality of <math>A</math> and <math>\omega</math> is the first infinite ordinal number. In particular, <math>\beth_{\alpha+1} = 2^{\beth_\alpha},</math>, and it follows by [[Cantor's theorem]] and transfinite induction that the sequence of beth numbers is strictly increasing. (<math>|A|^{|B|}</math> is the cardinality of the set of functions from <math>B</math> to <math>A</math>, so <math>2^{|B|}</math> is the cardinality of the [[power set]] of <math>B</math>.)

<math>\beth_0 = |V_\omega| = |\omega| = \aleph_0</math>. In general, <math>\beth_\alpha\not<\aleph_\alpha</math> for ordinal <math>\alpha</math>, and <math>\aleph_\alpha\leq\beth_\alpha</math> for every [[limit ordinal]] <math>\alpha</math>. The [[axiom of choice]] implies that the inequality holds in general.

The second beth number <math>\beth_1</math> is equal to <math>\mathfrak{c}</math>, the [[cardinality of the continuum]] (the cardinality of the set of the [[real number]]s), and the third beth number <math>\beth_2</math> is the cardinality of the power set of the continuum.

Like aleph numbers, beth numbers are idempotent: <math>\beth_\alpha^2 = \beth_\alpha</math>. This follows by transfinite induction from two points:

* <math>V_\lambda\times V_\lambda \subseteq V_\lambda</math> for every limit ordinal <math>\lambda</math>; and

* <math>(2^{\mathfrak{p}})^2 = 2^{2\mathfrak{p}} = 2^{\mathfrak{p}}</math> for every idempotent cardinal number <math>\mathfrak{p}\geq2</math>.

The axiom of choice implies that every set of cardinal numbers has a supremum and that for any set <math>\mathbb{S}</math>, the union set of all its members can be no larger than the supremum of its member cardinalities times its own cardinality. It follows (given the axiom) that <math>\beth_\lambda = \sup\Bigl\{ \beth_\alpha : \alpha < \lambda \Bigr\}</math> for every limit ordinal <math>\lambda</math>.

Note that this behavior is different from that of successor ordinals. Even with the axiom of choice, cardinalities less than <math>\beth_{\alpha+1}</math> but greater than <math>\beth_\alpha</math> can exist. (In that case, the existence is undecidable in ZFC and controlled by the [[Generalized Continuum Hypothesis]].)

== Relation to the aleph numbers ==
Even with the axiom of choice (provided Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory is consistent), little more is knowable about the relationship to aleph numbers than is stated above. For example, <math>\beth_1</math> cannot be <math>\aleph_\omega</math>, but there is a model in which <math>\beth_1=\aleph_{\omega+1}</math>.

Assuming the [[axiom of choice]], infinite cardinalities are [[total order|linearly ordered]]; no two cardinalities can fail to be comparable. Since <math>\beth_\alpha\not<\aleph_\alpha</math>, the axiom implies that 
<math>\beth_\alpha \ge \aleph_\alpha</math> 
for all ordinals <math>\alpha</math>.

Given the axiom of choice, the [[continuum hypothesis]] is equivalent to
:<math>\beth_1=\aleph_1.</math>
Without the axiom of choice, there are statements that address Cantor's concern about subsets of the real line without obviously implying that the real line admits a well ordering. For example, one version of the hypothesis is that <math>\mathfrak{p}\leq\beth_0</math> for every cardinal number <math>\mathfrak{p}<\beth_1</math>.

The [[Continuum hypothesis#Generalized continuum hypothesis|generalized continuum hypothesis]] extends the assertion above to other indices. One formulation says the sequence of beth numbers is the same as the sequence of [[aleph number]]s, i.e., 
<math>\beth_\alpha = \aleph_\alpha</math> 
for all ordinals <math>\alpha</math>. This assertion obviously implies the axiom of choice since beth numbers are cofinal. (In Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory, <math>A\subseteq V_{\omega+\alpha}</math> for some <math>\alpha</math>, so <math>|A| \leq |V_{\omega+\alpha}| = \beth_\alpha</math>. It follows from the statement that <math>|A| \leq \aleph_\alpha</math>, whence <math>A</math> admits a well ordering.) Different formulations of the continuum hypothesis suggest different generalizations, but the known 'reasonable' generalizations turn out to be equivalent and to imply the axiom of choice, although the proofs are more difficult.

== Specific cardinals ==

=== Beth null ===
Since (as noted above) this is equal to <math>\aleph_0</math>, or [[aleph null]], sets with cardinality <math>\beth_0</math> include:

* the [[natural number]]s <math>\mathbb{N}</math>
* the [[rational number]]s <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>
* the [[algebraic number]]s <math>\mathbb{A}</math>
* the [[computable number]]s and [[computable set]]s
* the set of [[finite set]]s of [[integer]]s or of [[rational number|rationals]] or of [[algebraic number]]s
* the set of [[Multiset|finite multiset]]s of [[integer]]s
* the set of [[finite sequence]]s of [[integer]]s.

=== Beth one ===

{{main|cardinality of the continuum}}

Sets with cardinality <math>\beth_1</math> include:

* the [[transcendental numbers]]
* the [[irrational number]]s
* the [[real number]]s <math>\mathbb{R}</math>
* the [[complex number]]s <math>\mathbb{C}</math>
* the [[uncomputable real number]]s
* [[Euclidean space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>
* the [[power set]] of the [[natural number]]s <math>2^\mathbb{N}</math> (the set of all subsets of the natural numbers)
* the set of [[sequence]]s of integers (i.e., <math>\mathbb{Z}^\mathbb{N}</math>, which includes all functions from <math>\mathbb{N}</math> to <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>)
* the set of sequences of real numbers, <math>\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}</math> 
* the set of all [[real analytic function]]s from <math>\mathbb{R}</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>
* the set of all [[continuous function]]s from <math>\mathbb{R}</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math>
* the set of all functions from <math>\mathbb{R}</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with at most countable discontinuities
*the set of finite subsets of real numbers
*the set of all [[analytic function]]s from <math>\mathbb{C}</math> to <math>\mathbb{C}</math> (the [[holomorphic]] functions)
*the set of all functions from the natural numbers to the natural numbers (<math>\mathbb{N}^\mathbb{N}</math>).

=== Beth two ===
<math>\beth_2</math> (pronounced ''beth two'') is also referred to as <math>2^\mathfrak{c}</math> (pronounced ''two to the power of <math>\mathfrak{c}</math>'').

Sets with cardinality <math>\beth_2</math> include:

* the [[power set]] of the set of [[real number]]s, so it is the number of [[subset]]s of the [[real line]], or the number of sets of real numbers
* the power set of the power set of the set of natural numbers
* the set of all [[function (mathematics)|functions]] from <math>\mathbb{R}</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> (<math>\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{R}</math>)
* the set of all functions from <math>\mathbb{R}^m</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math>
* the set of all functions from <math>\mathbb{R}</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with uncountably many discontinuities
* the power set of the set of all functions from the set of natural numbers to itself, or the number of sets of sequences of natural numbers
* the [[Stone–Čech compactification]]s of <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>, and <math>\mathbb{N}</math>

=== Beth omega ===
<math>\beth_\omega</math> (pronounced ''beth omega'') is the smallest [[uncountable]] [[strong limit cardinal]].

==Generalization==
The more general symbol <math>\beth_\alpha(\kappa)</math>, for ordinals <math>\alpha</math> and cardinals <math>\kappa</math>, is occasionally used. Given the axiom of choice, it is defined by:
:<math>\beth_0(\kappa)=\kappa,</math>
:<math>\beth_{\alpha+1}(\kappa)=2^{\beth_\alpha(\kappa)},</math>
:<math>\beth_\lambda(\kappa)=\sup\{ \beth_\alpha(\kappa):\alpha<\lambda \}</math> if ''λ'' is a limit ordinal.

Without the axiom of choice, the definition is more complicated. The main difficulty is that the cardinalities of infinite disjoint unions cannot be calculated just from the cardinalities of the components. Still using recursion, define <math>W_\alpha(A)</math> as follows:
:<math>W_0(A)=A,</math>
:<math>W_{\alpha+1}(A) = \mathcal{P}(W_\alpha(A)),</math>
:<math>\beth_\lambda(A) = \bigcup_{\alpha\in\lambda}(\{\alpha\}\times W_\alpha(A))</math> if ''λ'' is a limit ordinal.

Given an injection <math>f:A\to B</math>, we can construct recursively injections <math>g_\alpha:W_\alpha(A)\to W_\alpha(B)</math>. If <math>f</math> is a bijection then so is <math>g_\alpha</math>, so we can define the mapping for cardinal numbers by <math>\beth_\alpha(|A|) = |W_\alpha(A)|</math>.

It follows (easily with the axiom of choice or after more meticulous argument otherwise) that
:<math>\beth_{\omega+\alpha}(0) = \beth_\alpha,</math>
where <math>\beth_\alpha</math> is an ordinary beth number, and
:<math>\beth_\beta(\beth_\alpha(\mathfrak{p})) = \beth_{\alpha+\beta}(\mathfrak{p}).</math>

In particular, <math>\beth_\alpha = \beth_\alpha(\beth_\omega(0)) = \beth_\alpha(\beth_0) = \beth_\alpha(\aleph_0)</math>. For any cardinal <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> and any ordinal number <math>\alpha\supseteq\omega^2</math>, <math>\beth_\alpha(\mathfrak{p}) \geq \beth_\alpha(0) = \beth_{\alpha-\omega} = \beth_\alpha</math>. On the other hand, <math>\mathfrak{p}\leq\beth_\beta</math> for some <math>\beta</math>, and it follows that <math>\beth_\alpha(\mathfrak{p}) \leq \beth_\alpha(\beth_\beta) = \beth_{\beta+\alpha} = \beth_\alpha</math> for large <math>\alpha</math> (e.g. the ordinality of <math>\omega</math> copies of <math>\beta</math> stacked linearly). Thus for every cardinal number <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> there is an ordinal number <math>\alpha_0</math> such that
:<math>\beth_\alpha(\mathfrak{p}) = \beth_\alpha</math> for every ordinal number <math>\alpha\supseteq\alpha_0</math>.

This also holds in Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with [[ur-element]]s (with or without the axiom of choice), provided that the ur-elements form a set which is equinumerous with a [[pure set]] (a set whose [[transitive set#Transitive closure|transitive closure]] contains no ur-elements). If the axiom of choice holds, then any set of ur-elements is equinumerous with a pure set. (If <math>A</math> is not equinumerous with any pure set then it is not clear what object of set theory would be its cardinality, let alone <math>\beth_\alpha(|A|)</math>. However, we can still construct <math>W_\alpha(A)</math> as above, and if <math>B</math> is equinumerous with <math>A</math> then <math>W_\alpha(B)</math> is equinumerous with <math>W_\alpha(A)</math>.)
